item.title: 先想「这句该怎么念」再出声：Inworld TTS-2 让语音模型学会表达决策，首包中位 46ms、难句读对率 93.4% ｜ Realtime TTS-2 updates: reasoning, speed and consistency
item.description:
一句话：第一个会先写「表演提示」再朗读的语音模型：短句快 13%、中句快 9%，27 个模型里首包最快。

要点：

  • 推理式语音：TTS-2 先读文本与上下文，写一句简短的「表达方向」（delivery direction），再按这个方向表演——作者称这是首个带推理的语音模型
  • 速度：短句生成快约 13%、中等长度快约 9%；Realtime TTS-2 Flash 首包中位 46 ms，在 Cekura 的 27 个模型里排最快（全文一次性送入）
  • 一致性：难读条目（hard items）正确读出率 93.4%——这类指标直接对应游戏里人名、术语与情绪的稳定表现

为什么值得看：NPC 语音的两个致命问题是「语气不对」和「读错」，而这两件事在纯端到端 TTS 里几乎无解。Inworld 的思路是先让模型显式决定「怎么念」，再合成——这层中间的语义决策，恰好是游戏侧可以干预的地方（给角色情绪、给场景上下文）。

中文摘要：Inworld 给 Realtime TTS-2 推送两项更新。第一项是推理：TTS-2 会先读文本与随附上下文，写出一句简短的表达方向，再按这个方向把台词说出来——官方称这是首个带推理的语音模型。第二项是速度与一致性：短句生成快约 13%、中等长度快约 9%；Realtime TTS-2 Flash 的首包中位延迟为 46 毫秒，在 Cekura 评测的 27 个模型中排最快（全文一次性送入）；难读条目的正确读出率为 93.4%。对游戏 NPC 来说，这三项指标分别对应「语气对不对」「能不能实时接话」「生僻词会不会读错」，比通用语音评测更贴近落地需求。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：Inworld AI（English）

原文发布：2026-10-28

本期推送：2026-10-30

Key results1stspeech model with reasoning: it decides how to say a line before saying it~13%faster generation on short utterances, ~9% on mid-length46 msmedian first audio for Realtime TTS-2 Flash, ranked fastest of 27 models by Cekura (full text sent upfront)93.4%of hard items read correctly by Realtime TTS-2

Today we're shipping two updates to Realtime TTS-2. Reasoning makes it the first speech model that decides how to say a line before saying it: TTS-2 reads the text and any context you send, writes a short delivery direction, then performs it. An updated model generates speech faster, matches reference voices more closely and holds steady across long sessions and long text.

Both run behind the same public model ID, 

inworld-tts-2
. The update reaches existing integrations automatically as it rolls out by serving region; Reasoning is opt-in, one field on the request.

01How it works

Speech models read the text they're given, and nothing tells them how it should sound. In a consumer app, your LLM generates every reply at runtime, so there's no one to add that direction by hand. A line like "I can't believe you did that." can mean delight, hurt or disbelief, and without context the model gives each of them the same neutral read.

Reasoning adds one step before synthesis, inside the same TTS-2 request:

There's no extra service to call or host. The reasoning step is a language model whose only job is to write the delivery direction for TTS-2. The direction comes back in the API response, and any instructions or tags you set yourself take precedence.

02Why it beats emotion tags

Emotion tags are a fixed list. Something has to pick a label like 

[happy]
for each line, usually your own LLM following prompt rules, and the voice plays that label. Reasoning writes a free-form direction instead, like warm, delighted, speaking through a smile, so a single read can set emotion, tone and pacing together, based on the context you pass.

Saves time

No tag vocabulary in your prompt, no rules to maintain, no scripts to tag by hand. Enable it and pass the context you already have.

Sounds more natural

Each line gets a direction based on its context, so delivery varies the way a person's does instead of switching between a few preset emotions.

03Try it today

Enable Reasoning in the request and pass context in its own field. Context shapes the delivery but is never spoken. The response includes the generated direction, so you can log it alongside the input and adjust your context when a read is off.

Request
curl -X POST https://api.inworld.ai/tts/v1/voice \
  -H "Authorization: Basic $INWORLD_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @- <<'JSON'
{
  "text": "I can't believe you did that.",
  "voiceId": "Reed",
  "modelId": "inworld-tts-2",
  "synthesisContext": {
    "reasoning": "REASONING_ON",
    "reasoningContext": "A friend has arranged an unexpected reunion."
  }
}
JSON
Response
{
  "audioContent": "UklGRiQAAABXQVZFZm10...",
  "usage": { "processedCharactersCount": 29, "modelId": "inworld-tts-2" },
  "reasoningInstruction": "Breathless and stunned, like a friend seeing a long-lost face."
}

Reasoning runs on TTS-2 synthesis, streaming and async requests. That suits audio you generate per message or ahead of time, like voice messages from a companion, generated stories and lessons, audiobooks, or pre-generated character lines. WebSocket streaming, duplex (including the Realtime API) and batch synthesis are coming soon.

For parameters and limits, see the Reasoning documentation.

04Faster generation across utterance lengths

The updated model addresses the failures that become apparent across real workloads. A voice application can move from a short acknowledgment to a detailed explanation, then read a date or confirmation code aloud. A companion might continue that exchange for an entire session. Across those, a voice can gradually change, a word can be skipped in a long passage, or a consonant lost at the end of a sentence.

In our comparisons with the previous version of TTS-2, short utterances are about 13% faster to generate, and mid-length utterances are about 9% faster. Generation speed is also more consistent across input lengths. That matters for applications whose responses vary in length: a voice agent may acknowledge a request in a few words before giving a longer explanation, and a tutor may move between a quick correction and a full worked example.

These figures describe TTS generation performance. The response delay a listener experiences also depends on turn detection, language model generation, network transit, and playback buffering. Measure those components separately when evaluating your application's latency.

05More consistent voices and more reliable speech

The updated model improves voice similarity in Stable mode, particularly for voices that have been difficult to clone accurately, and reduces voice drift during long duplex sessions. Custom voices stay closer to the reference speaker, while companions and voice agents maintain a more consistent identity as the conversation develops.

It also fixes cases where TTS-2 skipped words in long utterances or dropped plosives on some word endings. Preserving these consonants, such as /p/, /t/, and /k/, makes affected word endings clearer. For audiobooks and articles read aloud, complete readings preserve the source text; for language learners and callers, clear pronunciation makes spoken details easier to understand.

Creative mode now produces more natural delivery, with light built-in steering. For interactive characters and companions, this improves how a line is performed as well as how the voice sounds. Use Stable mode when voice consistency is the priority, and test Creative mode where a more expressive performance fits the experience. The audio generation documentation explains the available delivery modes.

Evaluate these improvements across full passages and extended sessions, with the lines your application actually generates. Compare cloned voices with their references, listen to samples from the beginning and end of a conversation for drift, and check generated speech against the source for omitted words or unclear endings. Assess these separately from naturalness and expressiveness.

06Independent benchmarks for speed and accuracy

Cekura's independent benchmark provides context for the TTS-2 family. Its results, updated October 28, 2026, distinguish TTS-2 from Realtime TTS-2 Flash:

  • Realtime TTS-2 Flash: 46 ms median, 73 ms p90 to the first audible sound, with the complete text supplied upfront. Cekura ranks that the fastest of the 27 models it tested in the non-streaming category. Its word-by-word input test is a separate measure.
  • Realtime TTS-2: 93.4% of difficult items read correctly, across numbers and shorthand, codes and addresses, words that depend on context, and medical terms.

    • Cekura times the first result from the moment the full sentence is sent to the first audible sound. The accuracy result is estimated from speech-to-text transcripts rather than human listening. Every model read the same 104 agent sentences, three times each, from one US East cloud region; see the methodology. These are results for the models Cekura tested, before this update and without Reasoning. The 13% and 9% speed improvements above come from our comparison of the updated and previous models.

    07Keep your integration and hear the difference

    If you already use 

    inworld-tts-2
    , continue using your existing integration. The update rolls out behind that identifier, with no API migration and no price change. Reasoning is opt-in: nothing changes in your audio until you enable it on a request.

    Try the updated model on the inputs that matter to your product: a difficult reference voice in Stable mode, an extended duplex conversation, or a long passage that previously lost words. If you have saved baseline audio, use the same text, voice, and settings to make the comparison useful. Then enable Reasoning on a few lines with the context your app already has, and compare the reads.

    For a repeatable evaluation, the Inworld TTS Open Evaluation Toolkit provides per-sample measurements and reports that let you inspect the errors behind aggregate scores. Combine transcript checks with listening tests on your production voices and languages.

    Same model ID, same price, better speech.Hear the updated model on your own text, then enable Reasoning on your next request.

    Start buildingRead the TTS docs→

item.title: 别让自回归毁掉预训练先验：Mix Forcing 用双向+自回归混合注意力做因果预训练，四步模型也能超过纯 TF 基线 ｜ Mix Forcing: Causal Pre-Training via Mixture Attention for Interactive World Models
item.description:
一句话：把双向注意力留在里面保视觉先验，同时用 teacher forcing 学下一个 chunk，再蒸馏成少步模型。

要点：

  • 问题很具体：交互式视频世界模型必须自回归生成，但把预训练的双向视频扩散模型直接用 teacher forcing 改造成自回归，会破坏它的视觉先验、拉低自回归质量
  • Mix Forcing 用「双向 + 自回归」混合注意力（MoBA）同时训练：自注意力里既用 teacher forcing 学因果的下一个 chunk 预测，又保留双向注意力维持预训练先验，得到一个强的因果初始化
  • 在线文本交互用 chunk 级交叉注意力：每个视频 chunk 条件在一个共享环境 prompt 上；消融显示 chunk 级 prompt 相比全局 prompt 能同时降低三类相机误差，四步模型也比只用 teacher forcing 的基线更好

为什么值得看：「微调成自回归就变糊」是世界模型落地时最常见的退化，这条给出的是训练侧的解法：不要把双向注意力扔掉，而是让它和因果预测共存。对要做少步实时世界模型（DMD/蒸馏那条线）的团队，这层因果初始化是前置条件。

中文摘要：交互式视频世界模型必须自回归生成，但把预训练的双向视频扩散模型直接用 teacher forcing 改造成自回归，会破坏其视觉先验并降低生成质量。Mix Forcing 提出一种因果预训练范式，用「双向与自回归混合注意力」（MoBA）同时训练：在自注意力里，一部分走 teacher forcing 学因果的下一 chunk 预测以支持自回归 rollout，另一部分保留双向注意力以维持预训练视觉先验，从而得到更强的因果初始化，供少步后训练使用。为支持在线文本交互，它还采用 chunk 级交叉注意力，让每个视频 chunk 条件在一个共享环境 prompt 上。消融显示 chunk 级 prompt 相比全局 prompt 能同时降低三类相机误差，四步蒸馏模型也优于纯 teacher forcing 基线。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-24

本期推送：2026-10-30

Mix Forcing: Causal Pre-Training via Mixture Attention for Interactive World Models

Abstract

While interactive video world models require autoregressive generation, directly adapting pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into autoregressive ones with teacher forcing can disrupt their visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality. In this paper, we introduce Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (MoBA) attention. Mix Forcing jointly trains a video diffusion model with both teacher forcing and bidirectional training, yielding a strong causal initialization for few-step post-training. In self-attention, Mix Forcing leverages teacher forcing to learn causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while using bidirectional attention to preserve pretrained visual priors. To support online text interaction, Mix Forcing further adopts a chunk-wise cross-attention design that conditions each video chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, without exposing future instructions to the current chunk. Following causal pre-training on a 14B image-to-video model, we apply consistency and distribution matching distillation to obtain a four-step autoregressive generator. Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks, including WBench and SANA-WM-Bench, show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control. Notably, our model supports high-fidelity long-horizon generation without quality degradation even over one-hour rollouts.

Project Page: https://zelingao98.github.io/mixforcing

1 Introduction

Interactive video world models [19, 34, 10, 49, 53, 33, 14, 47], which predict future states conditioned on historical context and user inputs, have shown great potential for world simulation, video gaming, and embodied intelligence. Since users act based on past observations, each video chunk must be generated without access to future frames or future instructions, which calls for causal autoregressive generation.

Recent works [34, 53, 14] build upon pretrained video diffusion models to leverage their strong visual priors. However, these priors are learned for bidirectional generation, where all frames are jointly denoised with access to both past and future frames. Some methods [16, 43] directly distill bidirectional models into few-step causal generators via ordinary differential equation (ODE) initialization and distribution matching distillation (DMD), but the trajectories of the bidirectional teacher depend on future information, preventing the causal student from converging to the target flow map. To address this, other methods [54, 50] first adapt pretrained models into many-step causal models with teacher forcing before few-step distillation, making this causal pre-training stage the foundation of the final generator.

However, teacher forcing departs from the pretraining setting of bidirectional video diffusion models in two aspects. In attention, each chunk attends only to its history rather than the full video; in noise level, each noisy chunk is predicted from clean historical context rather than jointly denoised with other chunks at a shared noise level, which encourages velocity prediction to over-rely on clean context. Both deviations disrupt pretrained visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality. Moreover, causal pre-training methods typically condition the whole video on a single global prompt, which exposes future events to the current chunk. Streaming methods  [40] support prompt updates by recaching the history under each new prompt, which rewrites the context of past frames.

In this paper, we introduce Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (MoBA) attention block. The key idea of Mix Forcing is to mix teacher forcing and bidirectional training: teacher forcing learns causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while bidirectional training retains the pretraining setting in both attention and noise level, preserving pretrained visual priors during causal adaptation. In addition, Mix Forcing conditions each teacher forcing chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, enabling online text interaction without exposing future instructions to the current chunk or recomputing the KV cache of past chunks.

Based on Mix Forcing, we build an interactive video world model with camera control and online text interaction (Fig.1). Starting from a 14B image-to-video model, we perform causal pre-training with Mix Forcing, and then apply consistency distillation (CD) [31] and DMD to obtain a four-step generator for KV-cached autoregressive rollout (Fig.2). Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control, and sustains high-fidelity generation over one-hour rollouts. Ablation studies further show that Mix Forcing provides a stronger initialization for few-step post-training than teacher forcing alone.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose the MoBA attention block, which mixes teacher forcing and bidirectional training to preserve pretrained visual priors during causal adaptation, with chunk-wise prompt conditioning for online text interaction.

  • •

    We build an interactive video world model through causal pre-training with Mix Forcing and few-step post-training with CD and DMD, supporting camera control, online text interaction, and four-step KV-cached autoregressive rollout.

  • •

    Experiments on internal and public benchmarks show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control.

    • 2 Related Work

    Interactive and Controllable Video World Models.

    Interactive world models predict visual states conditioned on user actions [3, 1, 36], while controllable video generation also supports text instructions and camera trajectories. Prior work incorporates camera geometry through ray representations [12, 13, 51], trajectory embeddings [37, 2], or relative positional encodings [20], enabling geometry-aware viewpoint control in video generation. Vid2World [15] adapts pretrained video diffusion for autoregressive action control, while LongLive [40] supports streaming prompt updates by recaching the history under each new prompt. MotionStream [30] supports interactive motion control during streaming video generation. Other video world models support interactive or long-horizon generation [45, 4, 14, 33, 34, 53, 10, 49]. In this work, we aim to use causal pre-training for interactive video world models, maintaining the visual priors of pretrained video diffusion models while enabling online text interaction through chunk-wise conditioning.

    Causal Autoregressive Video Generation.

    Autoregressive video models generate frames or chunks sequentially [8, 35], with some using KV-cached streaming inference [29, 19]. FramePack [46] compresses historical frames for long rollouts, while diffusion-forcing approaches assign varying noise levels across video frames [5, 38, 6]. To adapt pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models for online video rollout, prior methods initialize few-step causal students from probability-flow ODE trajectories [32, 18, 43] and subsequently improve them through distribution matching distillation [41]. Self Forcing [16] addresses rollout errors using self-generated history; Self-Forcing++ [7] and Self Gradient Forcing [55] extend this approach through teacher supervision on long self-generated rollouts and context-gradient reconstruction, respectively. Resampling Forcing [11] and Rolling Forcing [23] use self-resampling and joint denoising, respectively. Causal Forcing [54] and Causal Forcing++ [50] improve few-step distillation using a causal teacher and causal consistency distillation, respectively. Reward Forcing [25] uses reward-weighted distribution matching distillation for streaming video generation. In Mix Forcing, we jointly optimize teacher forcing and bidirectional attention during causal pre-training to retain pretrained visual priors before few-step post-training.

    3 Methodology

    In this section, we present Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models. We first review flow matching and teacher forcing for interactive video modeling (Sec.3.1). We then introduce the MoBA attention block that implements Mix Forcing, which mixes teacher forcing and bidirectional training to preserve pretrained visual priors, with chunk-wise prompt conditioning for online text interaction (Sec.3.2).     3.3 Mix Forcing for Interactive Video World Models

    Causal Pre-Training.

    We initialize our interactive video world model from a pretrained bidirectional video model and apply Mix Forcing for causal pre-training. For camera control, we represent the camera pose eᵢ of chunk i with Plücker embeddings [12, 13], which encode the viewing ray of each pixel as six-dimensional coordinates. Following [10, 34], we inject them through adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) [39] without disrupting the pretrained visual priors. During causal pre-training, we jointly train our model with camera-labeled and unlabeled data. For unlabeled data, we use an all-zero dummy Plücker embedding as the condition input. As a result, a bidirectional video diffusion model is converted into an interactive video model supporting camera control and multi-step autoregressive rollout with KV cache.

    4 Experiments

    In this section, we first detail the experimental setup, including benchmarks, evaluation metrics, and implementation details (Sec.4.1). We then compare our model with state-of-the-art video world models quantitatively (Sec.4.2) and qualitatively (Sec.4.3). Finally, we conduct an ablation study to validate the design of MoBA and the effect of Mix Forcing on few-step post-training (Sec.4.4).

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Benchmarks.

    We construct an internal benchmark (InBench) to evaluate event-following ability and camera-control precision. We use GPT-Image 2.5 [27] to generate 96 initial images and organize InBench into two subsets: (i) an interactive subset covering environmental changes and character interactions (32 cases); and (ii) a roaming subset covering human characters and virtual objects (64 cases). Each case is evaluated with a video of 8 to 35 seconds, and each interactive case contains 3 to 5 prompt updates. We also evaluate on WBench [44] and SANA-WM-Bench [53].

    Evaluation Metrics.

    Following WBench and SANA-WM-Bench, we report aesthetic quality (AQ), imaging quality (IQ), temporal flickering (TFlk), and dynamic degree (DD) from VBench [17], HPSv3 [26], and rotation error (Rot, in radians), translation error (Trans), and camera-motion consistency (CMC) between the input and estimated camera trajectories. For long rollouts, IQ_a--b denotes imaging quality from a to b seconds, and sustained imaging quality (SIQ) averages the first and last windows. For online text interaction, we use a vision-language model as a judge [52] to measure Event Adherence (EA), the completion of each event, and On-Time Accuracy (OT), whether a correct response appears within a given time after each prompt update (see Appendix).

    Implementation Details.

    We train on 100k self-collected clips (974 hours), 70% of which have camera poses estimated by COLMAP [28], while the rest use the dummy Plücker embedding (Sec.3.3). For causal pre-training, we initialize from Wan2.1-I2V-14B-480P, train on variable-length 480×832 videos at 16 FPS with λ_TF=λ_BID=1, and use AdamW with a learning rate decaying from 5e-5 to 1e-5; the chunk sizes for teacher forcing and chunk-wise cross-attention are 1 and 4 latent frames, respectively. We randomly perturb the clean context latents using low-level noise with 50% probability [19]. For post-training, CD uses LPIPS [48] as the distance metric with a learning rate of 2e-6, and DMD follows LingBot-World-Fast with LingBot-World-Base [34] as score models. All three stages use 256 H20 GPUs, with 15k, 8k, and 1.5k steps for pre-training, CD, and DMD.

    4.2 Quantitative Comparison

    Evaluation on InBench.

    Tab.1 shows that our model achieves the best average quality, event-following, and camera-control results among all methods. The highest average quality score of 75.1 indicates that Mix Forcing preserves pretrained visual priors during causal pre-training, and the event-following scores (EA=94.4, OT1.5s=96.8) validate that chunk-wise cross-attention enables effective responses to online prompts. The lowest camera errors further demonstrate precise camera control during autoregressive rollout.

    Evaluation on Public Benchmarks.

    We report SANA-WM-Bench results in Tab.2. On both the simple and hard 60-second splits, our model achieves the highest average Quality (74.8 and 74.7) and SIQ (66.7 and 66.4) scores, whereas several baselines show clear quality drops in later windows, e.g., the IQ of LingBot-World-Fast decreases from 63.2 to 52.0 on the simple split. These results demonstrate that our model maintains visual fidelity throughout minute-long autoregressive generation; one-hour qualitative results and average quality scores measured every five minutes are further provided in Figure. S12 in the Appendix. Although competitive, our camera errors are not the lowest on SANA-WM-Bench. We partly attribute this gap to a prompt mismatch: the benchmark describes the entire video with a single global prompt, whereas our model is trained with an environment prompt and chunk-wise local prompts. Although local prompts do not explicitly specify camera motion, they indicate what should appear in the current chunk and thus help the pose condition control viewpoints more precisely, as supported by the reduced camera errors with chunk-wise prompts in Tab.4. We further evaluate on the Navi-158 subset of WBench (Table. S1 in the Appendix), where our model achieves the highest average Quality (78.5) and Setting adherence (80.3) scores, indicating strong visual fidelity and faithful reflection of the specified world settings, while its Interaction scores show a gap similar to that of the camera errors on SANA-WM-Bench.

    User Study.

    To complement these automatic metrics, we further conduct a pairwise user study. Participants compare our model with one baseline at a time in a method-blinded, side-by-side setting, rating visual quality on all cases, interactive following on the interactive subset, and motion clarity on the roaming subset. We collect 318 pairwise trials from 18 sessions, with details provided in the Appendix. As shown in Fig.4, participants consistently prefer our model over each baseline in terms of visual quality, interactive following, and motion clarity.

    4.3 Qualitative Comparison

    Camera-Controlled Roaming.

    Fig. 55(a) illustrates the qualitative comparison on the InBench roaming subset. During camera movement, especially when the viewpoint changes, the video model needs to generate the visual content from a novel perspective while keeping its structure and appearance stable across frames. We observe that existing state-of-the-art methods suffer from progressive blurring and structural distortion, recovering sharpness only after the camera stops moving. In contrast, the enlarged regions highlighted by yellow boxes show that our model better maintains scene consistency, motion clarity, and fine-grained appearance throughout the viewpoint transition.

    Online Prompt Interaction.

    Fig. 55(b) illustrates the qualitative comparison on the InBench interactive subset. Although JoyAI-Echo-WM and LingBot-World-Fast support prompt updates, we observe that they respond with noticeable delays, consistent with their lower OT1.0s in Tab.1, or disrupt existing scene content. In contrast, with the chunk-wise cross-attention in Mix Forcing, the enlarged regions highlighted by red boxes show that our model responds to each local prompt and generates the correct content while maintaining scene consistency.

    4.4 Ablation Study

    For the ablation study, we sample a subset of our internal training data with each video clip containing 161 frames and follow the training settings described in Sec.4.1. The evaluation is carried out on InBench, where we measure generation quality on the full benchmark, event-following ability on the interactive subset, and camera error on the roaming subset.

    Self-Attention Design for Causal Pre-Training.

    Using teacher forcing (TF) as the baseline, we evaluate the effects of adding diffusion forcing (DF) [5] and bidirectional (BID) training. As shown in Tab.3, TF+BID (row 4) improves generation quality, achieves the highest SIQ of 58.4, and maintains high final-window quality (from IQ0–2=55.9 to IQ8–10=61.0), while IQ drops from 51.5 to 48.3 under TF, indicating that bidirectional attention can mitigate quality degradation. However, adding DF (rows 2 and 3) can reduce generation quality. We attribute this degradation to a mismatch between training and inference, where DF uses noisy historical chunks during training, while KV-cached inference leverages fully denoised historical context. Note that DF replaces the clean history with independently noised history, which matches neither the clean KV cache at inference nor the shared noise level of pretraining. In contrast, MoBA keeps the clean history in TF for inference consistency and recovers the pretraining setting in a separate BID branch. We further study the effect of training chunk size under TF+BID. As chunk size=1 (row 4) enables fine-grained causal modeling by assigning an independent noise level to each latent frame and outperforms the other settings (rows 5 and 6) in both generation quality and camera control accuracy, we combine TF and BID training with chunk size=1 in MoBA.

    Cross-Attention Design for Causal Pre-Training.

    As shown in Tab.4, we study the effect of global and chunk-wise prompts in cross-attention. Chunk-wise prompts improve event-following ability, increasing EA from 23.4 to 50.0 and OT1.5s from 18.3 to 62.1. Chunk-wise prompts also reduce all three camera errors, consistent with our analysis in Sec.4.2.

    Mix Forcing for Few-Step Post-Training.

    As shown in Tab.5, we study the effect of pre-training with Mix Forcing on few-step post-training. Under the same CD and DMD pipeline, the four-step model pretrained with Mix Forcing (row 3) outperforms the TF-only baseline (row 2), indicating that Mix Forcing provides a stronger initialization. Compared with the 50-step model (row 1), the four-step model retains comparable generation quality and achieves higher event-following scores.

    5 Conclusion

    We present Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models. Implemented with the MoBA attention block, it mixes teacher forcing and bidirectional training to preserve pretrained visual priors, and uses chunk-wise prompts for online text interaction. Combined with CD and DMD, our four-step model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with camera control over one-hour rollouts.

    Limitations.

    Our implementation targets video DiT architectures with separate self-attention and cross-attention modules, and its extension to unified attention [21] remains to be verified. Moreover, our model is designed for chunk-wise local prompts, and its camera control is less precise when only a single global prompt is available, as observed on public benchmarks. We leave these directions for future work.

    Data Acquisition.

    We collect 100k video clips totaling 974 hours. We collect egocentric recordings, videos from games and Unreal Engine environments, and web videos. These sources cover first-person interactions, controlled synthetic scenes, and diverse real-world content.

A vision-language model assesses the remaining clips for editing artifacts, viewpoint, and interaction content.

    For each clip, we generate a shared environment prompt describing the scene and a global prompt summarizing the entire video. We separately annotate subject visibility, motion, interactions, and environmental changes, then combine the active annotations into local prompts. We refine these prompts for consistent wording and temporal alignment, removing descriptions of future events or actions unsupported by visual evidence. Each local prompt is shared by four consecutive latent frames, consistent with the cross-attention setting in the main paper.

    Camera Annotation.

    We estimate camera poses using COLMAP for 70% of the video clips. The remaining 30% are used without camera annotations, with all-zero Plücker embeddings as the conditioning input.

    A.2 Training Settings

    Causal Pre-Training.

    We initialize our model from Wan2.1-I2V-14B-480P and train on variable-length videos at 16 FPS with a resolution of 480×832. We train for 15k steps on 512 H200 GPUs using AdamW with a learning rate of 5×10⁻⁵ decaying to 1×10⁻⁵. TF and BID are jointly optimized in a single forward pass with equal loss weights, λ_TF=λ_BID=1.0. Under TF, we use chunk size=1 and independently sample a timestep for each latent frame, while BID uses a shared timestep for the entire video. We set the flow shift to 5. We perturb the clean historical context with low-level noise with 50% probability to improve robustness during autoregressive rollout [19].

    Consistency Distillation.

    We use the causal pre-trained model as the teacher to distill a four-step generator. We fully fine-tune the video backbone and camera-control modules, using chunk size=4 latent frames and conditioning on one initial frame. We optimize the student for 8k steps on 512 H20 GPUs using AdamW with a learning rate of 2×10⁻⁶, (β₁,β₂)=(0,0.999), and no learning-rate warm-up. The target model is maintained as an exponential moving average of the student parameters with a decay rate of 0.99. We set N=48 for discrete CD and use a guidance scale of 3.0. We replace use LPIPS as CD loss.

    Distribution Matching Distillation.

    We further refine the four-step generator obtained from CD using DMD for 1.5k steps on 512 H20 GPUs. We retain the same four-step schedule with timestep indices {0,250,500,750}. We use LingBot-World-Base [34] for the real and fake score models. The real score model remains fixed, while the fake score model is updated with the standard diffusion loss on generated videos. The generator is optimized using the distribution matching objective described in the main paper. We set the learning rates to 2×10⁻⁶ for the generator and 4×10⁻⁷ for the fake score model, with (β₁,β₂)=(0,0.999) for both optimizers.     B.1 Quality and Camera-Control Metrics

    We adopt the quality metrics from VBench [17] and WBench [44], and the camera-error metrics from SANA-WM-Bench [53]. On InBench, quality is evaluated on the full benchmark, while camera errors are evaluated on the roaming subset. Quality scores are reported on a 0–100 scale, with higher values indicating better performance; lower camera errors indicate more accurate control.

    Aesthetic Quality (AQ).

    AQ evaluates the visual appeal of generated frames, including composition, color, and lighting. The LAION aesthetic predictor scores the normalized CLIP ViT-L/14 features of each sampled frame. We average these frame scores within each video and multiply the result by 10 to convert the original 0–10 scale to 0–100.

    Imaging Quality (IQ).

    IQ evaluates frame quality, including sharpness, noise, and visual artifacts. We use MUSIQ, a no-reference image-quality model, to score each sampled frame after resizing its longer edge to at most 512 pixels. The video score is the mean of the frame scores on the 0–100 scale.

    Temporal Flickering (TFlk).

    TFlk measures frame-to-frame appearance variation using the mean absolute pixel difference between consecutive evaluated frames. Let d̄ denote this difference averaged over frame pairs, spatial locations, and color channels, with pixel values in [0,255]. The score is TFlk=100(1-d̄/255), so a higher score indicates less flickering.

    Dynamic Degree (DD).

    DD measures the proportion of generated videos containing substantial motion. We estimate optical flow between consecutive sampled frames using RAFT and average the largest 5% of flow magnitudes for each pair. Following the official implementation, the motion threshold is 6\min(H,W)/256, where H and W are the frame dimensions after preprocessing. A video with N sampled frames is classified as dynamic if at least \max(1,round(N/4)) frame pairs exceed this threshold. DD is the percentage of videos classified as dynamic.

Mix Forcing: Causal Pre-Training via Mixture Attention for Interactive World Models

Abstract

While interactive video world models require autoregressive generation, directly adapting pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into autoregressive ones with teacher forcing can disrupt their visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality. In this paper, we introduce Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (MoBA) attention. Mix Forcing jointly trains a video diffusion model with both teacher forcing and bidirectional training, yielding a strong causal initialization for few-step post-training. In self-attention, Mix Forcing leverages teacher forcing to learn causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while using bidirectional attention to preserve pretrained visual priors. To support online text interaction, Mix Forcing further adopts a chunk-wise cross-attention design that conditions each video chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, without exposing future instructions to the current chunk. Following causal pre-training on a 14B image-to-video model, we apply consistency and distribution matching distillation to obtain a four-step autoregressive generator. Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks, including WBench and SANA-WM-Bench, show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control. Notably, our model supports high-fidelity long-horizon generation without quality degradation even over one-hour rollouts.

1 Introduction

Interactive video world models [19, 34, 10, 49, 53, 33, 14, 47], which predict future states conditioned on historical context and user inputs, have shown great potential for world simulation, video gaming, and embodied intelligence. Since users act based on past observations, each video chunk must be generated without access to future frames or future instructions, which calls for causal autoregressive generation.

Recent works [34, 53, 14] build upon pretrained video diffusion models to leverage their strong visual priors. However, these priors are learned for bidirectional generation, where all frames are jointly denoised with access to both past and future frames. Some methods [16, 43] directly distill bidirectional models into few-step causal generators via ordinary differential equation (ODE) initialization and distribution matching distillation (DMD), but the trajectories of the bidirectional teacher depend on future information, preventing the causal student from converging to the target flow map. To address this, other methods [54, 50] first adapt pretrained models into many-step causal models with teacher forcing before few-step distillation, making this causal pre-training stage the foundation of the final generator.

However, teacher forcing departs from the pretraining setting of bidirectional video diffusion models in two aspects. In attention, each chunk attends only to its history rather than the full video; in noise level, each noisy chunk is predicted from clean historical context rather than jointly denoised with other chunks at a shared noise level, which encourages velocity prediction to over-rely on clean context. Both deviations disrupt pretrained visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality. Moreover, causal pre-training methods typically condition the whole video on a single global prompt, which exposes future events to the current chunk. Streaming methods  [40] support prompt updates by recaching the history under each new prompt, which rewrites the context of past frames.

In this paper, we introduce Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (MoBA) attention block. The key idea of Mix Forcing is to mix teacher forcing and bidirectional training: teacher forcing learns causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while bidirectional training retains the pretraining setting in both attention and noise level, preserving pretrained visual priors during causal adaptation. In addition, Mix Forcing conditions each teacher forcing chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, enabling online text interaction without exposing future instructions to the current chunk or recomputing the KV cache of past chunks.

Based on Mix Forcing, we build an interactive video world model with camera control and online text interaction (Fig.1). Starting from a 14B image-to-video model, we perform causal pre-training with Mix Forcing, and then apply consistency distillation (CD) [31] and DMD to obtain a four-step generator for KV-cached autoregressive rollout (Fig.2). Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control, and sustains high-fidelity generation over one-hour rollouts. Ablation studies further show that Mix Forcing provides a stronger initialization for few-step post-training than teacher forcing alone.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose the MoBA attention block, which mixes teacher forcing and bidirectional training to preserve pretrained visual priors during causal adaptation, with chunk-wise prompt conditioning for online text interaction.

  • •

    We build an interactive video world model through causal pre-training with Mix Forcing and few-step post-training with CD and DMD, supporting camera control, online text interaction, and four-step KV-cached autoregressive rollout.

  • •

    Experiments on internal and public benchmarks show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control.

    • 2 Related Work

    Interactive and Controllable Video World Models.

    Interactive world models predict visual states conditioned on user actions [3, 1, 36], while controllable video generation also supports text instructions and camera trajectories. Prior work incorporates camera geometry through ray representations [12, 13, 51], trajectory embeddings [37, 2], or relative positional encodings [20], enabling geometry-aware viewpoint control in video generation. Vid2World [15] adapts pretrained video diffusion for autoregressive action control, while LongLive [40] supports streaming prompt updates by recaching the history under each new prompt. MotionStream [30] supports interactive motion control during streaming video generation. Other video world models support interactive or long-horizon generation [45, 4, 14, 33, 34, 53, 10, 49]. In this work, we aim to use causal pre-training for interactive video world models, maintaining the visual priors of pretrained video diffusion models while enabling online text interaction through chunk-wise conditioning.

    Causal Autoregressive Video Generation.

    Autoregressive video models generate frames or chunks sequentially [8, 35], with some using KV-cached streaming inference [29, 19]. FramePack [46] compresses historical frames for long rollouts, while diffusion-forcing approaches assign varying noise levels across video frames [5, 38, 6]. To adapt pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models for online video rollout, prior methods initialize few-step causal students from probability-flow ODE trajectories [32, 18, 43] and subsequently improve them through distribution matching distillation [41]. Self Forcing [16] addresses rollout errors using self-generated history; Self-Forcing++ [7] and Self Gradient Forcing [55] extend this approach through teacher supervision on long self-generated rollouts and context-gradient reconstruction, respectively. Resampling Forcing [11] and Rolling Forcing [23] use self-resampling and joint denoising, respectively. Causal Forcing [54] and Causal Forcing++ [50] improve few-step distillation using a causal teacher and causal consistency distillation, respectively. Reward Forcing [25] uses reward-weighted distribution matching distillation for streaming video generation. In Mix Forcing, we jointly optimize teacher forcing and bidirectional attention during causal pre-training to retain pretrained visual priors before few-step post-training.

    In this section, we first detail the experimental setup, including benchmarks, evaluation metrics, and implementation details (Sec.4.1).     4.1 Experimental Setup

    Benchmarks.

    We construct an internal benchmark (InBench) to evaluate event-following ability and camera-control precision. We use GPT-Image 2.5 [27] to generate 96 initial images and organize InBench into two subsets: (i) an interactive subset covering environmental changes and character interactions (32 cases); and (ii) a roaming subset covering human characters and virtual objects (64 cases). Each case is evaluated with a video of 8 to 35 seconds, and each interactive case contains 3 to 5 prompt updates. We also evaluate on WBench [44] and SANA-WM-Bench [53].

    Evaluation Metrics.

    Following WBench and SANA-WM-Bench, we report aesthetic quality (AQ), imaging quality (IQ), temporal flickering (TFlk), and dynamic degree (DD) from VBench [17], HPSv3 [26], and rotation error (Rot, in radians), translation error (Trans), and camera-motion consistency (CMC) between the input and estimated camera trajectories. For long rollouts, IQ_a--b denotes imaging quality from a to b seconds, and sustained imaging quality (SIQ) averages the first and last windows. For online text interaction, we use a vision-language model as a judge [52] to measure Event Adherence (EA), the completion of each event, and On-Time Accuracy (OT), whether a correct response appears within a given time after each prompt update (see Appendix).

    Implementation Details.

    We train on 100k self-collected clips (974 hours), 70% of which have camera poses estimated by COLMAP [28], while the rest use the dummy Plücker embedding (Sec.3.3). For causal pre-training, we initialize from Wan2.1-I2V-14B-480P, train on variable-length 480×832 videos at 16 FPS with λ_TF=λ_BID=1, and use AdamW with a learning rate decaying from 5e-5 to 1e-5; the chunk sizes for teacher forcing and chunk-wise cross-attention are 1 and 4 latent frames, respectively. We randomly perturb the clean context latents using low-level noise with 50% probability [19]. For post-training, CD uses LPIPS [48] as the distance metric with a learning rate of 2e-6, and DMD follows LingBot-World-Fast with LingBot-World-Base [34] as score models. All three stages use 256 H20 GPUs, with 15k, 8k, and 1.5k steps for pre-training, CD, and DMD.

    4.2 Quantitative Comparison

    Evaluation on InBench.

    Tab.1 shows that our model achieves the best average quality, event-following, and camera-control results among all methods. The highest average quality score of 75.1 indicates that Mix Forcing preserves pretrained visual priors during causal pre-training, and the event-following scores (EA=94.4, OT1.5s=96.8) validate that chunk-wise cross-attention enables effective responses to online prompts. The lowest camera errors further demonstrate precise camera control during autoregressive rollout.

    Evaluation on Public Benchmarks.

    We report SANA-WM-Bench results in Tab.2. On both the simple and hard 60-second splits, our model achieves the highest average Quality (74.8 and 74.7) and SIQ (66.7 and 66.4) scores, whereas several baselines show clear quality drops in later windows, e.g., the IQ of LingBot-World-Fast decreases from 63.2 to 52.0 on the simple split. These results demonstrate that our model maintains visual fidelity throughout minute-long autoregressive generation; one-hour qualitative results and average quality scores measured every five minutes are further provided in Figure. S12 in the Appendix. Although competitive, our camera errors are not the lowest on SANA-WM-Bench. We partly attribute this gap to a prompt mismatch: the benchmark describes the entire video with a single global prompt, whereas our model is trained with an environment prompt and chunk-wise local prompts. Although local prompts do not explicitly specify camera motion, they indicate what should appear in the current chunk and thus help the pose condition control viewpoints more precisely, as supported by the reduced camera errors with chunk-wise prompts in Tab.4. We further evaluate on the Navi-158 subset of WBench (Table. S1 in the Appendix), where our model achieves the highest average Quality (78.5) and Setting adherence (80.3) scores, indicating strong visual fidelity and faithful reflection of the specified world settings, while its Interaction scores show a gap similar to that of the camera errors on SANA-WM-Bench.

    User Study.

    To complement these automatic metrics, we further conduct a pairwise user study. Participants compare our model with one baseline at a time in a method-blinded, side-by-side setting, rating visual quality on all cases, interactive following on the interactive subset, and motion clarity on the roaming subset. We collect 318 pairwise trials from 18 sessions, with details provided in the Appendix. As shown in Fig.4, participants consistently prefer our model over each baseline in terms of visual quality, interactive following, and motion clarity.

    4.3 Qualitative Comparison

    Camera-Controlled Roaming.

    Fig. 55(a) illustrates the qualitative comparison on the InBench roaming subset. During camera movement, especially when the viewpoint changes, the video model needs to generate the visual content from a novel perspective while keeping its structure and appearance stable across frames. We observe that existing state-of-the-art methods suffer from progressive blurring and structural distortion, recovering sharpness only after the camera stops moving. In contrast, the enlarged regions highlighted by yellow boxes show that our model better maintains scene consistency, motion clarity, and fine-grained appearance throughout the viewpoint transition.

    Online Prompt Interaction.

    Fig. 55(b) illustrates the qualitative comparison on the InBench interactive subset. Although JoyAI-Echo-WM and LingBot-World-Fast support prompt updates, we observe that they respond with noticeable delays, consistent with their lower OT1.0s in Tab.1, or disrupt existing scene content. In contrast, with the chunk-wise cross-attention in Mix Forcing, the enlarged regions highlighted by red boxes show that our model responds to each local prompt and generates the correct content while maintaining scene consistency.

    4.4 Ablation Study

    For the ablation study, we sample a subset of our internal training data with each video clip containing 161 frames and follow the training settings described in Sec.4.1. The evaluation is carried out on InBench, where we measure generation quality on the full benchmark, event-following ability on the interactive subset, and camera error on the roaming subset.

    Self-Attention Design for Causal Pre-Training.

    Using teacher forcing (TF) as the baseline, we evaluate the effects of adding diffusion forcing (DF) [5] and bidirectional (BID) training. As shown in Tab.3, TF+BID (row 4) improves generation quality, achieves the highest SIQ of 58.4, and maintains high final-window quality (from IQ0–2=55.9 to IQ8–10=61.0), while IQ drops from 51.5 to 48.3 under TF, indicating that bidirectional attention can mitigate quality degradation. However, adding DF (rows 2 and 3) can reduce generation quality. We attribute this degradation to a mismatch between training and inference, where DF uses noisy historical chunks during training, while KV-cached inference leverages fully denoised historical context. Note that DF replaces the clean history with independently noised history, which matches neither the clean KV cache at inference nor the shared noise level of pretraining. In contrast, MoBA keeps the clean history in TF for inference consistency and recovers the pretraining setting in a separate BID branch. We further study the effect of training chunk size under TF+BID. As chunk size=1 (row 4) enables fine-grained causal modeling by assigning an independent noise level to each latent frame and outperforms the other settings (rows 5 and 6) in both generation quality and camera control accuracy, we combine TF and BID training with chunk size=1 in MoBA.

    Cross-Attention Design for Causal Pre-Training.

    As shown in Tab.4, we study the effect of global and chunk-wise prompts in cross-attention. Chunk-wise prompts improve event-following ability, increasing EA from 23.4 to 50.0 and OT1.5s from 18.3 to 62.1. Chunk-wise prompts also reduce all three camera errors, consistent with our analysis in Sec.4.2.

    Mix Forcing for Few-Step Post-Training.

    As shown in Tab.5, we study the effect of pre-training with Mix Forcing on few-step post-training. Under the same CD and DMD pipeline, the four-step model pretrained with Mix Forcing (row 3) outperforms the TF-only baseline (row 2), indicating that Mix Forcing provides a stronger initialization. Compared with the 50-step model (row 1), the four-step model retains comparable generation quality and achieves higher event-following scores.

    5 Conclusion

    We present Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models. Implemented with the MoBA attention block, it mixes teacher forcing and bidirectional training to preserve pretrained visual priors, and uses chunk-wise prompts for online text interaction. Combined with CD and DMD, our four-step model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with camera control over one-hour rollouts.

    Limitations.

    Our implementation targets video DiT architectures with separate self-attention and cross-attention modules, and its extension to unified attention [21] remains to be verified. Moreover, our model is designed for chunk-wise local prompts, and its camera control is less precise when only a single global prompt is available, as observed on public benchmarks. We leave these directions for future work.

    Supplementary Material

    Visual comparison results are available at https://zelingao98.github.io/mixforcing.

    Supplementary Contents

    Appendix A Implementation Details

    A.1 Training Data

    Data Acquisition.

    We collect 100k video clips totaling 974 hours. We collect egocentric recordings, videos from games and Unreal Engine environments, and web videos. These sources cover first-person interactions, controlled synthetic scenes, and diverse real-world content.

    Data Filtering.

    We split videos at shot boundaries and remove clips with decoding errors or unsuitable duration and resolution. We further filter clips using visual quality, exposure, text occupancy, and motion statistics. A vision-language model assesses the remaining clips for editing artifacts, viewpoint, and interaction content.

    Prompt Annotation.

    For each clip, we generate a shared environment prompt describing the scene and a global prompt summarizing the entire video. We separately annotate subject visibility, motion, interactions, and environmental changes, then combine the active annotations into local prompts. We refine these prompts for consistent wording and temporal alignment, removing descriptions of future events or actions unsupported by visual evidence. Each local prompt is shared by four consecutive latent frames, consistent with the cross-attention setting in the main paper.

    Camera Annotation.

    We estimate camera poses using COLMAP for 70% of the video clips. The remaining 30% are used without camera annotations, with all-zero Plücker embeddings as the conditioning input.

    A.2 Training Settings

    Causal Pre-Training.

    We initialize our model from Wan2.1-I2V-14B-480P and train on variable-length videos at 16 FPS with a resolution of 480×832. We train for 15k steps on 512 H200 GPUs using AdamW with a learning rate of 5×10⁻⁵ decaying to 1×10⁻⁵. TF and BID are jointly optimized in a single forward pass with equal loss weights, λ_TF=λ_BID=1.0. Under TF, we use chunk size=1 and independently sample a timestep for each latent frame, while BID uses a shared timestep for the entire video. We set the flow shift to 5. We perturb the clean historical context with low-level noise with 50% probability to improve robustness during autoregressive rollout [19].

    Consistency Distillation.

    We use the causal pre-trained model as the teacher to distill a four-step generator. We fully fine-tune the video backbone and camera-control modules, using chunk size=4 latent frames and conditioning on one initial frame. We optimize the student for 8k steps on 512 H20 GPUs using AdamW with a learning rate of 2×10⁻⁶, (β₁,β₂)=(0,0.999), and no learning-rate warm-up. The target model is maintained as an exponential moving average of the student parameters with a decay rate of 0.99. We set N=48 for discrete CD and use a guidance scale of 3.0. We replace use LPIPS as CD loss.

    Distribution Matching Distillation.

    We further refine the four-step generator obtained from CD using DMD for 1.5k steps on 512 H20 GPUs. We retain the same four-step schedule with timestep indices {0,250,500,750}. We use LingBot-World-Base [34] for the real and fake score models. The real score model remains fixed, while the fake score model is updated with the standard diffusion loss on generated videos. The generator is optimized using the distribution matching objective described in the main paper. We set the learning rates to 2×10⁻⁶ for the generator and 4×10⁻⁷ for the fake score model, with (β₁,β₂)=(0,0.999) for both optimizers. The fake score model is updated at every training step, while the generator is updated once every five steps.

    Appendix B Evaluation Details

    B.1 Quality and Camera-Control Metrics

    We adopt the quality metrics from VBench [17] and WBench [44], and the camera-error metrics from SANA-WM-Bench [53]. On InBench, quality is evaluated on the full benchmark, while camera errors are evaluated on the roaming subset. Quality scores are reported on a 0–100 scale, with higher values indicating better performance; lower camera errors indicate more accurate control.

    Aesthetic Quality (AQ).

    AQ evaluates the visual appeal of generated frames, including composition, color, and lighting. The LAION aesthetic predictor scores the normalized CLIP ViT-L/14 features of each sampled frame. We average these frame scores within each video and multiply the result by 10 to convert the original 0–10 scale to 0–100.

    Imaging Quality (IQ).

    IQ evaluates frame quality, including sharpness, noise, and visual artifacts. We use MUSIQ, a no-reference image-quality model, to score each sampled frame after resizing its longer edge to at most 512 pixels. The video score is the mean of the frame scores on the 0–100 scale.

    Temporal Flickering (TFlk).

    TFlk measures frame-to-frame appearance variation using the mean absolute pixel difference between consecutive evaluated frames. Let d̄ denote this difference averaged over frame pairs, spatial locations, and color channels, with pixel values in [0,255]. The score is TFlk=100(1-d̄/255), so a higher score indicates less flickering.

    Dynamic Degree (DD).

    DD measures the proportion of generated videos containing substantial motion. We estimate optical flow between consecutive sampled frames using RAFT and average the largest 5% of flow magnitudes for each pair. Following the official implementation, the motion threshold is 6\min(H,W)/256, where H and W are the frame dimensions after preprocessing. A video with N sampled frames is classified as dynamic if at least \max(1,round(N/4)) frame pairs exceed this threshold. DD is the percentage of videos classified as dynamic.

    Human Preference Score v3 (HPSv3).

    HPSv3 estimates human visual preference using a learned reward model. Following WBench, we evaluate up to 20 uniformly sampled frames per video with empty text prompts and average their raw rewards to obtain r̄. We use the fixed normalization bounds from the official implementation:

    HPSv3=100clip ((r̄-r_low)/(r_high-r_low),0,1), r_low=-5.21, r_high=8.61.

    		(S1)

    These bounds are shared across models and are not re-estimated for each model.

    Quality Average.

    We average the per-video scores of each metric over the evaluated videos. The Quality score reported in the comparison and ablation tables is the arithmetic mean of the five metrics:

    Quality=AQ+IQ+TFlk+DD+HPSv3/5.

    		(S2)

    Temporal IQ and Sustained Imaging Quality (SIQ).

    Temporal IQ evaluates how imaging quality changes during autoregressive rollout by applying the same IQ metric to different time windows. For the 10-second ablation videos, we evaluate the first and last two seconds, denoted by IQ₀₋₋₂ and IQ₈₋₋₁₀. For the 60-second SANA-WM-Bench videos, we use IQ₀₋₋₁₀ and IQ₅₀₋₋₆₀. In both settings, SIQ is the arithmetic mean of the first- and last-window IQ scores. We report both window scores alongside SIQ to show the change in quality over time.

    Camera Pose Estimation.

    Following SANA-WM-Bench, we estimate camera poses from generated videos using Pi3X and compare them with the input camera trajectories at corresponding frames. The trajectories are expressed relative to their first frame, and the estimated trajectory is aligned to the target trajectory in rotation, translation, and scale using the official evaluation procedure. Let (Rₖ,tₖ) and (R̂ₖ,t̂ₖ) denote the target and aligned estimated camera-to-world poses, respectively, for evaluated frame k. We compute the following errors over M evaluated frames and average the video-level results across videos.

    Rotation Error (Rot).

    Rot measures the angular difference between the estimated and target camera orientations. We report the mean geodesic rotation error in radians, consistent with the main-paper tables:

    Rot=1/M∑ₖ₌₁^M\arccos [clip ((tr(Rₖ^⊤R̂ₖ)-1)/(2),-1,1)].

    		(S3)

    Translation Error (Trans).

    Trans measures the positional difference between the aligned estimated and target camera centers. It is computed as Trans=1/M∑ₖ₌₁^M∥t̂ₖ-tₖ∥₂, in the coordinate scale of the target trajectory.

    Camera-Motion Consistency (CMC).

    CMC jointly measures rotation and translation errors using the difference between the full pose matrices. With Pₖ=[Rₖ|tₖ] and P̂ₖ=[R̂ₖ|t̂ₖ], we compute CMC=1/M∑ₖ₌₁^M∥P̂ₖ-Pₖ∥_F, where ∥·∥_F denotes the Frobenius norm.

    B.2 Event-Following Evaluation

    We evaluate event-following ability on the interactive subset of InBench using a vision-language model. For each requested event, the evaluator records its completion score and the timestamp of the first visible response. EA measures event completion, while OT_1.0s and OT_1.5s measure timely responses within 1.0 and 1.5 seconds, respectively.

    Evaluated Events.

    We evaluate local prompt updates after the initial prompt, excluding updates that reset the local prompt to the shared environment prompt. For event j in video c, let a_cj be its prompt-update time and b_cj the next prompt-update time, with b_cj=+∞ for the final update. Let T_c=(F_c-1)/f_c be the timestamp of the last valid frame, where F_c and f_c are the video frame count and frame rate. The event is evaluated within I_cj=[a_cj,b_cj)∩[0,T_c]. Thus, a new prompt update ends the preceding event interval, including when the new prompt resets to the environment description. We include an event only if a_cj

    Let J_c denote the number of evaluated events in video c, and let ℂ₊={c:J_c>0} denote the videos containing at least one such event. All methods use the same event definitions and evaluation videos. An event remains in the denominator even if the model does not respond.

    Event Adherence (EA).

    EA measures how completely the model performs the requested events. Using visual evidence within I_cj, the evaluator assigns

    s_cj=\begincases1,&the requested event is clearly completed, 0.5,&the event is recognizable but incomplete, 0,&the event is absent or incorrect.\endcases

    		(S4)

    Matching scene appearance, unrelated camera motion, or unchanged content from before the update alone does not count as event completion. We average the event scores within each video and then average equally across videos:

    EA=(100)/(|ℂ₊|)∑_c∈ℂ₊(1)/(J_c)∑ⱼ₌₁^J_cs_cj.

    		(S5)

    On-Time Accuracy (OT).

    OT measures whether the model responds correctly within τ seconds of a prompt update. Let r_cj be the timestamp of the first inspected frame within I_cj showing clear new evidence of the requested event. If no such response is observed, we set r_cj=+∞. The event receives timing credit only when the response occurs within both its active interval and the time threshold:

    q_cj^(τ)=1 [r_cj∈I_cj ∧ 0≤r_cj-a_cj≤τ],(S6)
    OT_τ=(100)/(|ℂ₊|)∑_c∈ℂ₊(1)/(J_c)∑ⱼ₌₁^J_cq_cj^(τ), τ∈{1.0s,1.5s},

    where 1[·] is the indicator function. We compute both OT scores from the same recorded response timestamps, measured in generated-video time rather than inference time. A response after the next prompt update receives no credit for the preceding event, even if it is within τ seconds of that event’s start. A recognizable partial response can receive OT credit without completing the event, so OT can exceed EA. Both metrics are reported on a 0–100 scale, with higher scores indicating better performance. Events have equal weight within each video, and videos have equal weight regardless of their number of events. Videos with J_c=0 are excluded rather than assigned zero scores; if ℂ₊ is empty, both metrics are reported as N/A.

    B.3 User Study

    We conduct a pairwise user study on InBench to evaluate visual quality, interactive following, and motion clarity.

    Pairwise Comparison.

    Each trial compares our model with one of five baselines: HY-WorldPlay, JoyAI-Echo-WM, LingBot-World-Fast, Matrix-Game 3.0, and SANA-WM-Streaming. The two videos use the same initial image and source control sequence and are displayed side by side at the same size using the 480p evaluation outputs. They are labeled only as Video A and Video B, with the left/right position of our model randomized independently for each trial. Model identities and numerical evaluation scores are hidden from participants.

    Case Allocation.

    The study uses the full InBench case pool, comprising 96 cases: 64 roaming cases and 32 interactive cases. Each session contains 20 pairs of videos (40 videos in total), corresponding to 10 interactive cases and 10 roaming cases, with no case repeated within a session. Each baseline appears in four trials per session. We shuffle the baseline assignments and select cases within each subset, prioritizing case–baseline pairs with fewer previous assignments. The two subsets are presented in separate blocks, and no case is repeated within a session.

    Evaluation Questions.

    For each applicable question, participants select Video A is better, They are the same, or Video B is better. The three evaluation dimensions are:

  • •

    Visual quality (both subsets). Participants compare overall appearance, temporal stability, natural motion, and visible artifacts.

  • •

    Interactive following (interactive subset). Participants compare how well the videos perform the requested events as the corresponding local prompts become active.

  • •

    Motion clarity (roaming subset). Participants compare scene detail during camera movement, focusing on blur, smearing, and ghosting. They judge frames during movement and select a tie when clarity is similar or no viewpoint change is visible.

    • Each trial therefore collects a visual-quality judgment and one judgment specific to its subset. Fig.S1 illustrates the evaluation interface.

    Preference Aggregation.

    We map the Video A/B choices back to model identities. For baseline b and question q, let W_bq, T_bq, and L_bq denote the numbers of answers preferring our model, a tie, and the baseline, respectively. With N_bq=W_bq+T_bq+L_bq, the reported preference rates are

    (Pᵒᵘʳˢ_bq,Pᵗⁱᵉ_bq,Pᵇᵃˢᵉ_bq)=(100)/(N_bq)(W_bq,T_bq,L_bq).

    		(S7)

    Each submitted answer has equal weight within its baseline–question group, and ties are retained as a separate outcome. We include completed trials from partially completed sessions and exclude unanswered questions. Visual-quality preferences combine judgments from both subsets, while interactive-following and motion-clarity preferences use only judgments from the interactive and roaming subsets, respectively.

    Appendix C Additional Experimental Results

    C.1 Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods

    Results on WBench.

    Tab.S1 reports the complete results on the Navi-158 subset of WBench [44], covering generation quality, setting adherence, and navigation performance. Our model achieves the highest average Quality and Setting scores of 78.5 and 80.3, respectively. It also obtains the highest AQ, IQ, HPSv3, and subject-adherence scores, indicating strong visual quality and adherence to the specified subjects. The average Interaction score is 84.3. We attribute this gap partly to a mismatch between the global prompts used in WBench and the chunk-wise prompt conditioning used in our cross-attention. This interpretation is supported by the cross-attention ablation in the main paper, where chunk-wise prompts reduce all three camera errors compared with global prompts.

    Results on SANA-WM-Bench.

    Tab.S2 provides the individual quality metrics on the Simple and Hard 60-second trajectory splits of SANA-WM-Bench [53], supplementing the average Quality scores reported in the main paper. Our model achieves the highest average scores of 74.8 and 74.7 on the two splits, respectively. On the Simple split, it also obtains the highest IQ and HPSv3 scores of 71.1 and 60.6. On the Hard split, it matches the highest DD score of 97.5 and achieves an HPSv3 score of 58.6, close to the best score of 58.8.

    Qualitative Comparison on InBench.

    Figs.S2 to S10 compare our interactive video world model with HY-WorldPlay, JoyAI-Echo-WM, Matrix-Game 3.0, SANA-WM-Streaming, and LingBot-World-Fast on 18 selected InBench cases. For each case, we show five frames at the same generated-video timestamps across all methods, with summaries of the active event instructions above the columns. For roaming cases, the five frames are sampled uniformly over the full video duration. The examples include environmental changes, character actions, and exploration across diverse scenes. In the portal, rainbow, and ocean-view room examples, our model responds to the requested events while retaining recognizable scene content. The roaming examples further illustrate subject and scene consistency during camera motion.

    C.2 Causal Pre-Training

    Fig.S11 presents 60-second rollouts from our causal checkpoint before few-step post-training. The eagle and fire-extinguisher comparisons show retained subject appearance and scene details at late timestamps, while the camera-controlled example further illustrates generation quality during exploration.

    C.3 Long-Horizon Generation

    Fig.S12 shows a one-hour rollout from our interactive video world model, traversing diverse environments from canals and city streets to indoor spaces and orbital views. We further evaluate the performance of one-hour rollouts, dividing each video into twelve consecutive five-minute intervals. For each interval, we compute the Quality score defined in Eq.S2 and report the mean and standard deviation across rollouts. The mean remains between 67.3 and 71.6, with a score of 69.3 in the final interval compared with 71.0 in the first, indicating relatively stable generation quality over one hour.

    C.4 Additional Interactive Results

    Figs.S13 and S14 present additional examples of online prompt interaction and camera-controlled exploration using our interactive video world model, illustrating changes in character actions and scene content in response to online prompts.

item.description:
一句话：Redstone SDK 2.4：4.1.2 的 INT8 模型覆盖 RDNA2 与 Ryzen AI Max，另配轻量模型给掌机。

要点：

  • 覆盖面：FSR Upscaling 4.1.2 的完整 INT8 模型从 RX 7000 扩到 RX 6000（RDNA2）与 Ryzen AI Max 300/400（RDNA3.5）；另有一个不到一半大小的轻量 INT8 模型，专为 Strix Point / Z2 系列这类受限核显准备，模型选择按硬件自动进行
  • Vulkan 首次与 DX12 功能对齐：FSR Upscaling 4.1.2、FSR Frame Generation 4.0.2、以及 3.1 系列都在 SDK DLL 层提供 Vulkan 支持，不依赖特定驱动版本；但「驱动自动升级」仍只对 DX12 游戏生效，Vulkan 游戏要自己集成到 4.1.2/4.0.2 才有资格
  • 其余更新：FSR Ray Regeneration 新增独立的环境光与高光遮蔽降噪；RX 9000 上的 Frame Generation 增加驱动辅助帧调度（Driver-Assisted Frame Pacing）

为什么值得看：两个数字值得记：轻量模型「不到一半大小」意味着核显与掌机终于能跑 ML 超分；Vulkan 与 DX12 对齐则意味着跨平台项目不必再为 AI 超分维护两套路径。做移动/掌机移植与跨 API 渲染后端的团队，这版是重新评估 FSR 的时间点。

中文摘要：AMD 发布 FSR「Redstone」SDK 2.4。核心变化是把 ML 超分下放：FSR Upscaling 4.1.2 的完整 INT8 模型在原有 RX 9000（FP8）与 RX 7000（INT8）之外，新增 RX 6000（RDNA2）与 Ryzen AI Max 300/400（RDNA3.5）支持；同时提供一个体积不到一半的轻量 INT8 模型，面向 Strix Point、Z2 Extreme 等受限核显，模型选择按目标硬件自动完成。Vulkan 首次与 DirectX 12 功能对齐，覆盖 FSR Upscaling 4.1.2、FSR Frame Generation 4.0.2 与 3.1 系列，能力由随游戏分发的 SDK DLL 提供，不依赖特定驱动版本；不过驱动层的自动升级仍只对 DX12 游戏生效。另外 FSR Ray Regeneration 新增独立的环境光与高光遮蔽降噪，RX 9000 上的帧生成加入驱动辅助帧调度。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：AMD GPUOpen（English）

原文发布：2026-10-28

AMD 发布 FSR「Redstone」SDK 2.4（原文 2026-10-28）。这一版的重点不是画质，而是覆盖面：把 ML 超分推到更老的独显与核显，并首次让 Vulkan 与 DirectX 12 功能对齐。

一、ML 超分下放到 RX 6000 与 Ryzen 核显

  • 6 月时，ML 版 FSR Upscaling 4.1 已扩到 RX 7000 系列；这次它也能跑在 RX 6000 系列（RDNA 2） 独显上；
  • 同时首次进入带 Radeon 核显的部分 Ryzen 处理器：Ryzen AI Max 300/400（Strix Halo / Gorgon Halo，RDNA 3.5 的 8000S）跑完整 INT8 模型；
  • 另有一个轻量 INT8 模型，体积不到完整模型的一半，专为受限核显准备：Strix Point / Gorgon Point 的 Ryzen AI 9 300/400、Z2 Extreme / Z2 A 等掌机与轻薄本芯片；
  • 模型选择按目标硬件自动完成，开发者不需要手写分支。官方提醒核显共享系统内存，超分表现会同时受内存带宽与整机功耗/散热影响。

二、Vulkan 首次与 DX12 功能对齐

FSR SDK 2.4 是第一个让以下效果在 Vulkan 上与 DirectX 12 功能对齐的 Redstone 版本：

  • FSR Upscaling 4.1.2、FidelityFX Super Resolution 3.1.6
  • FSR Frame Generation 4.0.2、FidelityFX SR Frame Generation 3.1.6、以及两者的 Swapchain 版本

关键细节：Vulkan 支持由随游戏分发的 SDK DLL 提供，不要求特定驱动版本；但「驱动层自动升级到更新版本」这件事仍只对 DX12 游戏生效——Vulkan 游戏要自己先集成 4.1.2 / 4.0.2 / Swapchain 4.0.0 及以上，之后才有资格走 Adrenalin 的自动升级。在 Vulkan 上，帧生成 swapchain 会替换应用的 VkSwapchainKHR，并返回 swapchain 创建、取图与 present 的替代函数指针。

三、其他更新

  • FSR Ray Regeneration 新增独立的环境光遮蔽与高光遮蔽降噪；
  • FSR Frame Generation 在 RX 9000 系列上获得驱动辅助帧调度（Driver-Assisted Frame Pacing）；
  • 本次 FSR Ray Regeneration 与 FSR Radiance Caching 仍是 DX12 专属。
